title: Closing arguments made in trial for Mountie involved in 2016 fatal collision
article: The court heard the closing arguments Thursday for a trial involving a Wood Buffalo RCMP officer who pled not guilty after she was charged in connection with a 2016 incident that ended with one man dead and another injured.
Crown prosecutor Douglas Taylor argued that Constable Michelle Phillips knew someone in dark clothing was walking in the driving lane of the highway and should have acted accordingly.
"This ought to have heightened the awareness of people on the highway," he said.

On the evening of Aug. 21, 2016, multiple witnesses said Tracy Lyle Janvier, 41, was walking down Highway 881, south of Anzac. Phillips was responding to a 911 call that a man matching Janvier's description was walking on the road.
Janvier was wearing all black clothing, while an autopsy found he was intoxicated.
As she approached the scene, Phillips accelerated when she was told Janvier had been hit by a truck. As she approached the scene, she was driving between 155 and 160 kilometres per hour.
On Wednesday, Phillips said dispatch told her the collision was approximately five to 10 kilometres from Anzac, when it was actually 30 kilometres south of the hamlet.

As she approached the scene, Phillips noticed several vehicles pulled over to the side of the road. Because she had her lights on, she assumed they had pulled over to get out of her way. It was not until the last second Phillips realized she was about to speed through the scene.
"I did not see anyone standing in the northbound lane," Phillips said in a recorded interview with investigators five days after the incident. "I was right on the body by the time I saw it."
James Cardinal, a passenger in the vehicle that first hit Janvier, was injured after the vehicle Phillips was driving hit his hand. He later required 30 stitches for his injuries.
Cardinal had gotten out of the vehicle to help Janvier and had called 911.
Phillips is charged with one count dangerous driving causing death and one count of dangerous driving causing bodily harm. In August 2017, she pleaded not guilty.

Defence lawyer Robb Beeman said he has no doubt she was driving fast, but argued that given the potentially life-threatening circumstances, "there is nothing that can be suggested she is driving in a dangerous manner." Beeman is asking for a full acquital.

Taylor acknowledged why Phillips began speeding to the scene, adding he did not think driving at 155 km/h on Highway 881 was "in and of itself" dangerous. However, he said a combination of several factors that changes things.

He argued Phillips knew she was approaching vehicles with flashing lights on. He also pointed out her windshield streaks made an "obvious glare" and she made no attempt to slow down, break or swerve as she approached the scene.
Before Phillips was posted in Wood Buffalo she was a dispatcher for four years and said Wednesday that sometimes locations given to officers can sometimes be inaccurate.
Knowing this, Taylor argued that she should have been more cautious when approaching what could have been the collision site, even if it was not the location given by dispatch.
"It would have taken seconds to slow down and clear hazards," he said. "She rockets through... all she had to do was take a few moments to assess that situation."

Beeman argued that Dr. Elizabeth Brooks-Lin, Alberta's chief medical examiner and the person who preformed the autopsy on Janvier, said it's possible Janvier could have still died from injuries sustained from the first collision. However, she added she could not say in what order he received each injury.
Beeman also argued that the court couldn't look at the matter with 20/20 hindsight.
"Ms. Phillips may have been wrong, but was her decision making unreasonable?"
